name: Content first
summary: Large, calm type and generous space, for people who come to read.
description: Content first is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Large, calm type and generous space, for people who come to read.

ai.avoid_when: Data-heavy tools or screens with many actions.

answers.why: Source Serif 4 for reading and headings, Inter for labels and captions: a good magazine's text with a quiet interface.

considers.readability: Source Serif 4 is a reading serif made for long text; its optical sizes keep body text open and even.
considers.legibility: Labels and captions sit in Inter, a sans with a tall x-height that stays clear at small sizes.
considers.scalability: Source Serif 4's optical sizes adjust the design from caption to display, so one family spans the scale.
considers.numerals: Data is rare here; numbers sit in the reading serif, set in running text rather than tables.
considers.scripts: Both cover Latin, Cyrillic and Greek; Hebrew and Arabic need another face, chosen to match.
considers.recognition: The brand shows in type, not in color, so the serif is the brand.
considers.familiarity: Serif text reads like a book or an article, which long-form readers know.
considers.personality: Warm and considered, as the brand answer asks.
considers.performance: Two variable families, one file each.
considers.licensing: SIL Open Font License, both: free to embed in apps and on the web.
considers.fallback: Falls back to Georgia and system-ui, as its tokens say; Inter is the serif's interface pair.

default.label: Content first
default.description: The single brand: deep navy ink on warm paper, a serif for reading.

theme.$description: The Content first theme: what each brand-dependent semantic key picks, in light and dark, plus mode-free picks (fonts, corners) in base. Info uses blue, kept apart from the brand color so it never reads as an action. Categories 1 to 5 are navy, blue, green, amber, stone: distinct hues for tags and chart series, with no meaning. Disabled uses the neutral stone.

open-ds.why: radius.8: We use an 8px corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a warm tone, by brand convention. A rounded radius does this by curving the edge enough to feel soft, while the sides stay straight. So controls feel friendly next to long text and never compete with it, because the brand is warm (brand.q1), corners are rounded (shape.values) and each screen holds one idea (content.q2).

radius.pill: We use a pill corner for badges in order to give status a role of its own, apart from the 8px controls. A full radius does this by rounding both ends into a capsule. So a status sits softly in the text and never reads as a button, because badges get their own corner (shape.roles) and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

radius.8: We use an 8px corner for menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 12px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by following the outer curve at the padding's distance. So an option's curve runs parallel to its menu's curve, because surfaces take 12px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the panel's padding is 4px (spacing.values).

radius.8: We use the 8px control corner for boxes that grow in order to keep their role, as objects of one family, by inheritance from the control corner. The same radius does this by giving a list item or a text area the curve of the controls beside it. So fields and rows read as one family, because the control corner is rounded, not a pill (shape.values), and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

radius.12: We use a 12px corner for article cards, menus and dialogs in order to make each card read as a separate object, in a warm tone by brand convention. A larger radius does this by breaking the outline with a curve wider than the 8px controls inside it. So a card reads as one calm object on the page, because containers get their own corner (shape.roles, shape.count) and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

shadow.none: We use no shadow for cards in order to keep them at the page's height: on the scale only floating layers rise. The missing shade does this by leaving the card flat, set apart by space. So reading flows down the page without boxes that lift, because only menus and dialogs float (elevation.roles) and shadows are soft (elevation.values).

shadow.overlay: We use step 2 of the shadow scale for menus and dialogs in order to show their height as floating layers. The cast shade does this by a 12px offset and a 32px blur in a 16% warm brown. So a menu lifts off warm paper without a hard edge, because only what floats rises (elevation.roles) and shadows are soft (elevation.values).

The lighter fill does this by the dark-mode depth rule: the higher a layer sits, the lighter its surface. So readers see a menu above the page even where its shadow barely shows, because dark ships as standard (theming.values) and the roles answer names the layers that rise (elevation.roles).

neutral.floor: We use the floor step, below the page's canvas, for table headers and wells in dark, in order to show depth by tone, 1.16:1 under content and 1.06:1 under the canvas. The darker fill does this by the depth rule turned downward: what sits lower is darker. So a well reads as recessed and never as a raised card, because dark ships as standard (theming.values) and depth reads from tone and lines (elevation.definition).

neutral.floor: We use the floor step, below the canvas, for the item under the pointer or the keyboard in dark, in order to mark it as a band on both surfaces it meets: 1.16:1 on surface.default and 1.39:1 on surface.raised, and 1.06:1 off the page. The fill does this by stepping darker, as raised layers took the lighter step; muted text still reads 7.15:1 on it. So the hovered row or menu item shows on cards and menus alike, because hover and focus have their own look (accessibility.roles) and the neutral ramp sets the steps (color.definition).

neutral.200: We use the step above the raised surface for a pressed item in dark in order to show a press as a change of its own. The fill does this by stepping lighter while the hover band steps darker, 2.04:1 from the highlight, so press and hover never match. So a tap reads under the finger, because pressed has its own look for touch (accessibility.roles) and the neutral ramp sets the steps (color.definition).

shadow.none: We use the light pick for the dark card elevation in order to keep the height it sets, and the step does this by the same means, so the dark card elevation and the light pick never differ, because the step reads the same in dark (theming.values).

shadow.overlay-dark: We use the light shadow's shape for menus and dialogs in dark in order to show the same floating height by the dark-shade relation. The cast shade does this by the same 12px offset and 32px blur, at 50% black instead of 16% brown. So a menu still lifts off the dark page, though its shade reads weaker on dark than in light, because only what floats rises (elevation.roles) and dark ships for night reading (theming.values).

neutral.why: A warm gray is calm, like paper, for long reading.

open-ds.why: Big, even steps give an 8px base. Spacious density doubles each gap: tight, default, group and section are 1, 2, 4 and 8 steps.

We use 8px for the tight gap between the parts of one item, such as an icon and its word, in order to group and separate: one base step (1 × 8px), the smallest of the big even steps. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So occasional readers see one item, not two, because steps are big and even (spacing.definition) and visitors see the interface fresh each time (human.q2).

We use 16px for the default gap between the items of one group in order to group and separate: two base steps (2 × 8px), twice the tight gap. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so each item in a list reads on its own, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and reading comfort is the measure (outcomes.q1).

We use 32px for the group gap between groups in a layout in order to group and separate: four base steps (4 × 8px), twice the default gap. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so the reader gets a place to pause between groups, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and people read from start to end (tasks.q1).

We use 64px for the section gap between page sections in order to group and separate: eight base steps (8 × 8px), twice the group gap. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so space alone separates sections, with no line to add noise, because the layout is spacious (spacing.values) and space is spent between paragraphs and sections (spacing.lands).

We use 20px for the inline padding inside controls in order to give content room inside its box: two and a half base steps (2.5 × 8px), wider than a table cell. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So each rare action has room and a button feels as calm as the text, because actions are rare (tasks.q2) and the brand is warm (brand.q1).

We use 24px for the padding inside cards and dialogs in order to give content room inside its box: three base steps (3 × 8px), half again the default gap. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so each card is framed like a page in a magazine, because the brand is warm (brand.q1) and reading comfort is the measure (outcomes.q1).

We use 16px for the inline padding inside table cells in order to give content room inside its box: two base steps (2 × 8px), the same as the default gap. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so cells get room like text does, and each row reads one by one, because people read from start to end (tasks.q1) and the layout is spacious (spacing.values).

A touch target sets the 48px default. Compact is one 4px step below it, 44px, the touch-size hit area itself; large equals the default, as actions are rare and calm. The scheme has no row role, so a row takes the default.

default.$description: Height of buttons and inputs, and the smallest target.

open-ds.why: We use 48px for buttons and inputs in order to make a hit target: the touch target size, step 0 of the control scale, a 48px hit area. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So readers on phones get a full touch target on every control, because the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values) and readers arrive on any device (scenarios.q1).

We use 44px for compact controls, such as a clear or show button inside a field, in order to make a hit target: one 4px step below the 48px default on the control scale, and a 44px box that is the touch-size hit area on its own. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so a small button fits inside the field around it, because the content is long-form text (content.q1) and the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values).

large.$description: Height of large controls. Not used in this system, so it equals the default.

open-ds.why: We use 48px for large controls in order to make a hit target: the default's step on the control scale and the default's 48px hit area, as the scheme has no hero action. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so a main action never shouts over the text, and color marks it, because actions are rare (tasks.q2) and attention belongs on the content (human.q1).

We use 48px for one table row in order to keep the eye on its row: by inheritance, as the scheme has no row role and a row holds controls, so size.row takes size.control.default, one 48px control tall. Row height does this by making each row a band the eye follows across, and a hit target when the row is clickable (WCAG 2.5.8: 24px). So a control fits in its row, and each row reads one by one, because spacing has gaps and insets only (spacing.roles) and the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values).
16px matches the 16px label text that icons sit beside in navigation, the one icon size this scheme uses.

hit-area.$description: The least hit area of a control. A control drawn smaller keeps its size; its hit area grows past it, never into a neighbour.

open-ds.why: We use a 44px hit area for controls drawn smaller, such as a checkbox, a radio or a switch, in order to make a hit target a fingertip can find: the WCAG 2.5.5 size. The hit area does this by growing past the drawn box through a pseudo-element, and rows in a group stand at least 44px apart, so no two targets overlap. So readers tap the right control on a phone, because targets are sized for touch (accessibility.values) and the layout leaves room for it (spacing.values).

badge.$description: Corner of badges, chips, tooltips, keyboard keys (kbd) and checkboxes: small labels and marks.

option.$description: Corner of options in menus and lists: the panel's corner less its padding, so the corners nest.

element.$description: Corner of an element that holds content and can grow past one line: a list item, an accordion row, a text area, a calendar, an attachment, a skeleton or media.

surface.$description: Corner of cards, menus and dialogs.

open-ds.why: We use a 1px default line for card and panel borders in order to give grouping where space alone does not, not separation: space separates groups here. A thin stroke does this by drawing a shared region with the least weight that still reads. So the lines stay quiet beside long text, because space separates groups (elevation.definition) and AA is the floor (accessibility.definition).

width.$description: The focus ring's width: one step heavier than the default border, and not a border width.

open-ds.why: We use a 2px focus ring in order to show focus, one step heavier than the 1px default line by the focus relation. A heavier stroke does this by standing out from the thin edges around it. So readers who use a keyboard always see where they are, because focus has its own look (accessibility.roles) and lines are thin (elevation.definition).

offset.$description: The gap between a control and its focus ring, so the ring never touches the control and reads on any fill.

open-ds.why: We use a fixed 2px focus offset in order to keep focus visible by contrast, not for style. The gap does this by showing the page color between ring and control, so one of the two colors keeps enough contrast against any fill (W3C technique C40). So readers see the ring on any fill, even a filled button, because focus has its own look (accessibility.roles).

Many fine steps: a large 18px body and a 1.12 ratio, with two steps between the headings, so long pages can set their own hierarchy. Headings sit tight at 1.15, labels and captions snug at 1.45, and body and data open to 1.65 for reading.

Display is 44px, eight fine steps above the 18px body (18 × 1.12^8 = 44.6), snapped to the 4px grid as headings are: two steps over the 36px title, kept for the landing moment and the lead that opens an article.
1.15 sets 44px display text on about 51px lines, so a two-line opener reads as one tight block.
600 lets the serif display carry the brand on the landing page, since the brand shows in type, not in color.
36px is six fine steps above body and two under the 44px display, so article titles stay large but calm.
1.15 sets a 36px title on about 41px lines, so a long article title wraps as one unit.
600 makes the serif article title the strongest line on an article page, without the landing-only display size.
28px is four fine steps above the 18px body and two under the 36px title, so readers find their place in a long guide.
1.15 keeps a 28px heading on about 32px lines, tighter than the 1.65 body, so it reads as one label for its section.
600 separates a serif section heading from 400 body text in the same family, so readers spot it while skimming.
18px is the large reading size and step 0 of the scale: every other role is a 1.12 ratio step from it, so long articles stay easy on the eyes.
1.65 gives 18px body text about 30px lines, so the eye finds the next line in a long paragraph.
400 is Source Serif 4's regular reading weight, so long text stays even and open across a whole article.
16px sets Inter labels one step under the 18px body (18 ÷ 1.12), still large enough for a field label people must read.
1.45, the snug ratio between the headings' 1.15 and body's 1.65: a 16px label gets about 23px lines, enough when a label wraps under zoom, without the airy body measure.
600 makes Inter labels firm beside the serif text, so a field label reads clearly where a caption would be too faint.
14px is two steps under the 18px body and one under the 16px label, for Inter captions that sit quietly under the text.
1.45, the snug ratio: a 14px caption under a figure or a quote gets about 20px lines, a step tighter than body so it reads as a note to the text, not more text.
400 keeps captions quiet: attention belongs to the article, so secondary notes take the regular weight.
18px shares step 0 with body, because numbers sit in running text rather than table columns, so data reads at the reading size.
1.65 matches body text, so a number set inside a paragraph keeps the 30px rhythm of the lines around it.
400 matches the reading serif's regular weight; data is rare, and a bolder number would pull attention from the text.

feedback.$description: Hover, press and toggle feedback. At most 150ms in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use 150ms (moderate) for hover, press and toggle feedback in order to confirm each action inside the productive limit of 150ms. The duration does this by ending the change before the eye leaves the control. So readers see each action land and never wait for it, because motion is for feedback and guidance, which makes the family productive (motion.roles), and feedback feels moderate (motion.values).

panels.$description: Menus, popovers, dialogs and drawers opening. At most 300ms in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use 300ms (relaxed) for menus, popovers, dialogs and other panels in order to show where a panel comes from, inside the productive limit of 300ms. The duration does this by giving the eye just enough frames to follow the panel from its trigger. So readers follow the new panel without losing their place in the text, because the family is productive (motion.roles) and there are two speeds (motion.count).

exit.$description: A layer closing. About 150ms, never more, in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use the feedback duration, 150ms (moderate), for a layer that closes in order to finish the exit move within the productive 150ms. The duration does this by removing the layer in fewer frames than an open takes, as nothing in it needs reading any more. So readers get the page back at once, because productive exits stay short (motion.roles) and there are two speeds (motion.count).

standard.$description: The transition move: a state that changes in place, such as hover, press or toggle.

open-ds.why: We use the standard easing (0.2, 0, 0, 1) for state changes in place in order to do the transition move. The curve does this by reaching its target early and settling slowly, with no overshoot. So a hover, a press or a toggle lands at once and then stays still, because easing is a standard ease-out (motion.definition) and the family is productive (motion.roles).

enter.$description: The enter move: a layer that appears.

open-ds.why: We use the transition move's standard easing for a panel that appears in order to do the enter move. The curve does this by spending most of the change in the first frames, so the layer is in place before it slows. So readers can read a menu almost as soon as it opens, because easing is a standard ease-out (motion.definition) in a productive family (motion.roles).

exit.$description: The exit move: a layer that closes in place.

open-ds.why: We use the strong-out easing (0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) for a layer that closes in place in order to do the exit move of the productive family. The curve does this by covering most of the way in the first third of its time, then easing to a stop. So a closed popover is gone before the next click, because productive exits take a strong ease-out (motion.roles) and easing never springs here (motion.definition).

exit-offscreen.$description: The exit move of a layer that slides off the screen: a sheet or a drawer.

open-ds.why: We use the exit move's strong-out easing for a drawer or sheet that slides off the screen, in order to keep every exit of a productive family on one fast curve. The curve does this by moving fastest at the start, so the panel clears the view with no slow tail. So the content under a closing sheet comes back at once, because only an expressive family accelerates what leaves the screen (motion.roles), and easing is a plain ease-out (motion.definition).

emphasize.$description: The emphasize move: a moment that calls for attention.

open-ds.why: We use the transition move's standard easing for a moment that calls for attention in order to give the emphasize move no overshoot. The curve does this by stopping at its target without passing it. So a new message draws the eye by its change, not by a bounce, because the family is productive (motion.roles) and easing is a standard ease-out, never a spring (motion.definition).

neutral.$description: The neutral scale: the scheme's gray, step by step. Surfaces, borders and text read it, never a gray directly.

highlight.$description: The item the pointer or the keyboard is on.

pressed.$description: The item while it is pressed.

scrim.$description: Dims the page behind a dialog.

on-light.$description: Text on any light fill, in either mode.

on-dark.$description: Text on any dark fill, in either mode.

info-on-light.$description: Info text on a light info fill, such as its tint in light mode.

info-on-dark.$description: Info text on a dark info fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

success-on-light.$description: Success text on a light success fill, such as its tint in light mode.

success-on-dark.$description: Success text on a dark success fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

warning-on-light.$description: Warning text on a light warning fill, such as its tint in light mode.

warning-on-dark.$description: Warning text on a dark warning fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

danger-on-light.$description: Danger text on a light danger fill, such as its tint in light mode.

danger-on-dark.$description: Danger text on a dark danger fill, such as its tint in dark mode.

raised.$description: The 1px edge of a raised layer: menus, dialogs and toasts, and raised cards.

selected.$description: The edge that marks a selected item, so selection is never color alone.

@.$description: The fill of a destructive commit: the confirm of a delete.
Info text and icons: neutral news, no action needed.
Category 1: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 2: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.

Category 4: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.
Category 5: chart series, tag dots and icons. Tag text uses color.text.primary.

category.$description: Colors with no meaning, for content that needs telling apart: decorative accents and non-semantic blocks such as tags, labels and chart series.

disabled.$description: The shared look of controls that cannot be used right now.

text.$description: Text and icons of a disabled control.

open-ds.why: Spacious: room around the text helps reading, so panels and fields breathe; rows stay tight.

stroke-width.$description: The line weight of every icon, on Lucide's 24px grid.

open-ds.why: A 1.5px stroke width is the outline style the icon answer names; a thin line keeps icons quiet beside the text.

Focus ring invalid of the input group.

radius.$description: Item radius of the radio group.
Group label radius of the sidebar.

Corner of the menu button, of the sidebar.
Corner of the switch's thumb: round, as the track is.

content.$description: Voice tokens: the words components use for common actions. Text, not CSS.

commit.$description: The label of the action that completes a task.

cancel.$description: The label of the way out next to the main action.

destroy.$description: The label of an action that deletes data.

retry.$description: The label that repeats a failed action.

empty-action.$description: The label of the action in an empty state.
